chapters.title: Chapter 1: The World's Stock Markets at a Glance

lessons.title: Developed, Emerging, and Frontier: How MSCI and FTSE Classify Markets

children.text: On Monday, 21 September 2026, two stock markets change labels. In FTSE Russell's indices, Vietnam moves up from frontier to emerging, and Greece moves up from emerging to developed. No Vietnamese company will have earned a single extra dong that morning. No Greek bank will have changed its balance sheet. Yet index funds around the world must buy or sell shares in both countries to match the new labels. An index provider decided which box each country belongs in, and billions of dollars move because of it. If you want to understand why foreign money flows into India or out of it, you need to understand these boxes.

body.text: A country's market label decides which global funds are allowed to own it. The label is set by index providers based on how easy the market is for foreigners to access, not just on how rich or large the economy is.

children.text: Who Draws the Map

markDefs.definition: A company that builds and maintains stock market indices and licenses them to fund managers. MSCI, FTSE Russell and S&P Dow Jones Indices are the three biggest global index providers.
The index a fund is measured against. A fund benchmarked to the MSCI Emerging Markets Index is judged on whether it beats that index, so its manager pays close attention to which countries are in it.

children.text: No government or regulator decides whether a stock market is developed or emerging. That job falls to
index providers

, mainly MSCI and FTSE Russell. Their classifications matter because trillions of dollars are managed against their indices. A pension fund in Canada or a sovereign fund in Norway tells its managers to invest in "emerging markets", and the manager picks an index as the
benchmark
. Whatever the index provider puts in that bucket is what the money buys.

children.text: The Tiers Explained

MSCI uses three main tiers: developed, emerging and frontier. Markets that do not fit any of them, usually because foreigners face severe restrictions, are put in a separate standalone category and kept out of the main indices. FTSE Russell splits emerging markets into two levels, advanced emerging and secondary emerging, giving it four tiers in total.

children.text: What MSCI Actually Checks
MSCI's framework rests on three pillars. Most people assume the first one, wealth, decides everything. In practice the third pillar, accessibility, is where most countries get stuck.

body.caption: MSCI's three pillars of market classification

cells: For developed status only: GNI per capita 25% above the World Bank's high-income threshold for three consecutive years
Rules out lower-income countries from developed status, however large their markets
A minimum number of companies meeting size and liquidity thresholds: 2 for frontier, 3 for emerging, 5 for developed
Funds need enough large, tradeable stocks to invest in
Openness to foreign ownership, ease of moving capital in and out, efficiency of trading and settlement, competitive landscape, stability of institutions
Decides whether a foreign fund can actually buy, hold, sell and take its money home

body.title: The five accessibility tests in plain language

children.text: Openness to foreign ownership.
Can foreigners buy shares freely, or do they face registration hurdles and caps on how much of a company they can own?
Ease of capital inflows and outflows.
Can money and currency move in and out without restrictions, and is the currency freely tradeable offshore?
Efficiency of the operational framework.
How smooth are account opening, trading, clearing, settlement and custody?
Competitive landscape.
Are market data, index products and investment instruments freely available, without exchange-imposed restrictions?
Stability of the institutional framework.
Are rules predictable, or can governments suddenly impose capital controls or freeze foreign holdings?
Same Market, Different Labels

Because MSCI and FTSE weigh the criteria differently, the same country can carry two different labels at the same time. South Korea is the most famous case. It has a rich economy, world-class companies like Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, and FTSE has treated it as developed since 2009. MSCI still calls it emerging. In its June 2026 review, MSCI said market participants still see the limited convertibility of the Korean won in offshore markets as a key barrier.

cells: Emerging, moving to Developed in May 2027
Moving to Secondary Emerging on 21 September 2026

body.text: Hong Kong is developed while mainland China is emerging, even though many of the same Chinese companies trade in both places. The difference is access. Hong Kong has a freely convertible currency, an open capital account and familiar legal rules. Mainland China still has capital controls and a managed currency. Classification follows the plumbing, not the flag.

body.title: Why is Korea still emerging for MSCI?
body.question: South Korea is a high-income economy with globally dominant companies. Based on MSCI's June 2026 review, what is the main reason it is still classified as an emerging market?
options: Its GNI per capita is below the World Bank's high-income threshold
It does not have enough large, liquid companies
Market accessibility, especially limited offshore convertibility of the Korean won
FTSE has already classified it as developed, so MSCI cannot
body.explanation: Korea easily passes the wealth and size tests. MSCI keeps it in emerging markets because of accessibility issues, with limited convertibility of the won in offshore currency markets named as a key barrier. FTSE's decision has no bearing on MSCI's. Each provider applies its own framework.

children.text: Where India Sits, and Why

India is an emerging market for MSCI and a secondary emerging market for FTSE, alongside China, Saudi Arabia and Indonesia. The reasons are worth knowing, because they are the same frictions that shape how FPIs deal with Indian shares every day.

columns.label: Where India scores well
points: Size and liquidity: hundreds of large, heavily traded companies
Efficient trading and settlement on NSE and BSE, with T+1 settlement
Deep domestic institutional base of mutual funds and insurers

columns.label: What holds India back
points: Economic development: GNI per capita far below the high-income threshold, which alone rules out developed status
Foreign investors must register as FPIs with SEBI before investing
Sector-wise foreign ownership limits in areas like banking and defence
Capital account controls, with the rupee not fully convertible

markDefs.definition: An adjustment MSCI makes to a company's index weight based on how many of its shares foreigners can actually buy. A company near its foreign ownership limit gets a lower weight than its market cap alone would suggest.

children.text: Accessibility does not just affect India's label. It also affects individual company weights. MSCI applies a
foreign inclusion factor

that trims a stock's weight when foreigners can own only part of it. That is why Indian private banks with little room left for foreign investors can carry a smaller weight in MSCI indices than their size suggests, and why an increase in a sector's foreign ownership limit can trigger fresh FPI buying.

children.text: Why a Label Change Moves Money

Index funds and ETFs must hold exactly what their index holds. When a country is added, they must buy. When it is removed, they must sell. Active managers benchmarked to the index usually follow, because not owning a market that is now in their benchmark is a risky bet. The mechanics are simple: the flow equals the money tracking the index multiplied by the country's new weight.

body.latex: \text{Estimated flow} = \text{Assets tracking the index} \times \text{Change in country weight}
body.caption: A first estimate of the buying or selling triggered by an index change

body.title: Vietnam's FTSE entry
body.prompt: Vietnam enters the FTSE Emerging Index with a weight of 0.22%. Suppose $300 billion of funds track that index closely. Roughly how much money, in $ million, would they need to invest in Vietnamese shares?
body.explanation: $300 billion × 0.22% = $300 billion × 0.0022 = $0.66 billion, or $660 million. The $300 billion is an illustrative figure, not official FTSE data. For a market of Vietnam's size, that is meaningful new demand, which is why prices often rise in the months before an inclusion takes effect as traders try to get in ahead of index funds.

body.text: An upgrade is not always good news for flows. When Greece moves from emerging to developed, it stops being a mid-sized holding in emerging market funds and becomes a tiny holding in developed market funds. EM funds must sell, and developed funds buy only a sliver. Markets that are upgraded can see net selling in the short run, even though the long-term signal is positive.

body.title: MSCI's calendar
body.textWithBlank: MSCI announces the results of its annual market classification review every year in the month of ___.
body.explanation: MSCI publishes its annual market classification review in June, usually a few days after its Global Market Accessibility Review. FTSE Russell reviews its country classifications twice a year, with announcements after its March and September reviews.

body.title: What if India were upgraded?
body.scenario: Imagine that, years from now, FTSE Russell announces that India will be upgraded from secondary emerging straight to developed status. India is one of the largest markets in FTSE's emerging indices. In the developed indices, it would sit alongside the US, Japan and Europe. A friend who holds a Nifty 50 index fund says: "This is fantastic, foreign money will pour into India."
body.prompt: Explain what would likely happen to foreign flows into Indian shares around the upgrade, and why your friend may be only partly right.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Emerging market funds benchmarked to FTSE would have to sell Indian shares, because India would no longer be in their index. Since India is a large weight in emerging market indices, this selling could be very big.
2. Developed market funds would start buying India, but India would be a small weight next to the US and Japan, so their buying might not fully offset the EM selling in the short run.
3. The net effect around the change date could be selling pressure, as happens with many upgrades, including Greece's.
4. Over the long term, your friend has a point. Developed status signals easier access and lower perceived risk, which can attract a broader, more stable base of global investors and lower the cost of capital for Indian companies.
5. The realistic answer: expect volatility and possibly net outflows around the event, with the benefits showing up over years rather than days.

body.title: Track classification news like a professional
steps: Mark June in your calendar for MSCI's annual market classification review and accessibility review.
Mark March and September for FTSE Russell's country classification announcements.
Check which countries are on each provider's watch list for upgrades or downgrades.
When India is mentioned, read whether the issue is foreign ownership limits, capital flows or operations.
When a large emerging market is upgraded or added, estimate the flow using assets tracking the index multiplied by the weight change, and ask whether India's weight goes up or down as a result.

cards.definition: A firm such as MSCI, FTSE Russell or S&P Dow Jones Indices that builds indices and decides which countries belong in each market category.
The index a fund is measured against. Funds tend to hold countries in line with their benchmark's weights.
A smaller, less liquid market with significant access hurdles, held mainly by specialist funds. Vietnam is frontier in MSCI's framework.
An MSCI category for markets excluded from the main indices because of serious barriers, such as Argentina.
How easily foreign investors can enter, trade in, and exit a market. It is the pillar that holds back most emerging markets, including India.
MSCI's adjustment to a stock's index weight based on how much of it foreign investors are allowed to own.
FTSE Russell's lower emerging market tier, which includes India, China, Saudi Arabia and Indonesia.

points: Index providers such as MSCI and FTSE Russell, not governments, decide whether a market is developed, emerging or frontier.
These labels matter because trillions of dollars are benchmarked to their indices. Over $1.8 trillion is benchmarked to MSCI's emerging market indexes alone.
MSCI judges economic development, size and liquidity, and market accessibility. Accessibility is where most countries get stuck.
The same market can carry different labels: South Korea is developed for FTSE but emerging for MSCI, largely because of limited offshore convertibility of the won.
India is emerging for MSCI and secondary emerging for FTSE, held back by lower income levels, FPI registration, sector ownership caps and capital account controls.
Label changes force index funds to buy or sell. Estimate the flow as assets tracking the index multiplied by the change in weight.
Upgrades can trigger short-term net selling, as emerging market funds exit a market that becomes a tiny weight in developed indices.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Classifications, country weights and review outcomes are drawn from MSCI and FTSE Russell announcements and published reports as of the dates stated, and may change. Flow estimates are illustrative. Countries and companies named are examples, not recommendations.
